All it is saying if you move group from B to C, the directly opposing group would now be C--if it exists.  If the opponent  does not have a Group C, then there would be no directly opposing group to your Group C.  (Just like there would be if each side set up with a different number of groups at start.)

I wonder whether having declared the intention to lateral group transfer a player can change their mind? 

I would say no per errata on Rule 5:  Movement cards not played directly to the discard pile cannot voluntarily be cancelled.  (Just like you can't rotate a Movement card from advancing to sideways because you change your mind about advancing.)

results.title: AFV questions (stun effect, etc.)
results.query:
AFV questions (stun effect, etc.): Background:  I have been playing Up Front for over 40 years, but I never liked AFV's and so avoided them.  Now I'm trying to use them more, and this has raised some questions that I didn't have to think about before.

Is a stunned, non-OT AFV forced to button up?  I think I had always assumed the answer was "yes", but re-reading the rules yesterday, I wasn't sure.  The clearest rule I can find is 28.45, which says, "A stun result flips any CE AFV card over to its Pinned/Button Up side."

Well, that is ambiguous.  It says it's only referring to CE AFVs, but then it mentions a Buttoned Up side, which a CE AFV does not have.  I think on the whole that I would find it odd that regular AFV's don't button up when stunned when OT AFV's do, but that's not much of a guide to go on.

I'd like to follow this up with a dumb question about boxed attacks.  I'm pretty sure I understand them, but they seem weird, so I just wanted to verify.  In brief:  when you shoot a boxed effect number against an AFV, you know exactly what's going to happen if you hit.  You simply add your boxed number to your relative range, and compare that to the defending AFV's numbers.  (There are exceptions for rifleman using inherent boxed FP at range 5 and for LATW.)  This feels weird to me because everything else in Up Front is accompanied by massive amounts of randomness, so for a hit's result to be absolutely known (with the possible exception of an immobilization or stun in case they have the same effect number) seems incongruous.  I just want to make sure I'm getting it right.

[28.45] A Stunned AFV, whether open-topped or not, is required to button up. This is explicitly stated in Rule 28.45, which mentions that a Stun result flips any CE AFV card over to its Pinned/Button Up side. Although the rule specifically refers to CE AFVs, the mention of the "Button Up" side implies that all AFVs, including non-CE ones, must button up when stunned.

Regarding boxed attacks, your understanding is correct. [28.4] When you use a boxed effect number to attack an AFV, the result is determined by comparing the sum of your boxed number and the relative range to the defending AFV's numbers. This process does indeed reduce the randomness typically associated with other attacks in Up Front. The exceptions you mentioned, such as riflemen using inherent boxed FP at range 5 and LATW, are correctly noted.

results.ground_truth_answer:
Couple of things - about getting AFVs to button up, one way for infantry to reduce the threat of an AFV is to fire at it with small arms, hoping to get a hit equal to or higher than its Morale value, which forces it to button up.  This is covered by 28.3:

An AFV card has two Armor defense values printed on each side of the card plus a Morale and CE Defense value on the front of the card. The Armor and Flank defense values represent the armored defense strength and is listed on both sides of the card; only attacks using solely boxed firepower or boxed "Effect Numbers" apply to this value. The MORALE and CE values are affected only by unboxed attack values.

This is how mortars can attack AFVs (and they have a small chance of damaging the vehicle as well [26.5]).  AT guns have the choice of firing AP - the process the OP referred to in his second question, which attacks the Armor/Flank values - or HE, which attacks the Morale value as above.  The HE attack is only possible, of course, when the vehicle is CE, or in the case of an OT vehicle if it is not already Pinned (except for one or two really weedy AFVs like the British Bren Carrier, which has a Panic value and can thus be attacked when Pinned).

And moving on to the OPs second question, you were right to feel that there should be a random element is resolving an AP hit - and there is!  25.4 says:

Once a hit has been obtained, the strength of that hit is determined by adding the To Hit Random Number on the RNC just drawn to the Effect Number listed on the ordnance card. (EXC: IG/AFV ordnance firing at an AFV target does not add the To Hit Random Number just drawn; instead it adds a number equal to the Relative Range between the firer and the target.)  The color of the RNC has no effect; all numbers are added. Having now determined the total strength of the attack (after modification for terrain and/or movement), it is resolved separately for each target in the defending group by drawing a new RNC and adding any black number or subtracting any red number drawn as per a normal fire attack [6.5]. 

So the Hit process establishes first whether a hit has been obtained, and secondly how damaging it is: for HE, the RNC on the To Hit card is used (provided a 0 would have hit, reflecting how close the HE round actually landed), and for AP a hit is a hit, but the RR is added to reflect increased penetration at closer ranges.  This gives you the base hit strength; then, in both cases, you draw an RNC for each target.  Firing at an AFV, of course, there is only one target, but you still draw an RNC.

So, a Panther (s7,i8,k9) rumbles up to RR4 to a plucky British 6-pdr (FE 3).  If the AT gun gets a hit, its base Hit Strength will be 3+4=7, and then it hopes the RNC will be at least 0, and preferably a black 2 or better to get a kill.

Don't forget, also, that unlike small arms and HE fire against an AFV, terrain does affect the resolution.  So if the AFV is in Brush, the Hit Strength is reduced by 1.  I suppose this reflects the possibility of the round being deflected or slowed by intervening obstacles.

Hope all that helps!  Oh, and Snipers are good, too.

 It gives an example (modified slightly to make better example for this question).

JP:  A(0)  B(0)

The Japanese player has the option to cancel a Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no longer directly opposite or adjacent),  or if another enemy moves in such a way as to block the access of the Banzai group to the declared target.

The Japanese are allowed to cancel a Banzai only if a position arises where it would not be legal to declare it. Lateral Group Transfer (17.7) = lateral movement of a group from Group B to Group C (for example).  (This should be called "Lateral Movement".)  This is initiated by playing a Movement card in sideways mode while declaring the Lateral Movement.  (I generally put the new group marker on the movement card). -  Group ID they are transferring to must be vacant.
-  Two or more men must be transferred at the same time to initiate Group Creation.

But they're wildly inaccurate in terms of actually representing the value of the cards in play. In practice most of the vehicles and IGs in the game are unusable in DYO because the points don't reflect their actual value (they overate armor and boxed firepower, which are rarely relevant in play in practice, as well as secondary weapons).

Infantry Guns are once of the dicier elements of the game. IGs as antitank weapons represent poor play value; tank duels are just not very compelling in Up Front. They are only used in scenario H, not one of the better scenarios in the game. The DYO values for these weapons are particularly useless in practice.

In practice, here is what I bet happened: the Up Front team came up with a formula for valuing guns and tanks which everyone knew was not particularly precise. Then they just playtested scenario F (or whatever) until they got it close, and they reverse-engineered the DYO template value for the scenario from their inaccurate AFV valuations. Scenario F's victory conditions are very close to A; the defender "wins ties", but that's not such a large advantage that you would think the attacker needs a huge 471:279 point force advantage in F compared to 241:241 for A. The DYO value of the attacker's force is wildly inflated because the tank is overpriced. This is why in free-form DYO scenarios like the 501 City Fight in 4 you only ever see a tiny number of vehicles, the ones where the point value formula AH came up with back in the day happened to produce a value that was actually kind of close (so, not heavily armored, no boxed firepower, no secondary weapon).

So here is my takeaway from all of these observations. If you want to expand the game to new IGs and new tanks, the best ones to do are actually not the AT guns that Avalon Hill focused on - I'd start with infantry guns or heavy mortars. The NRA had a variety of older infantry guns and smaller artillery pieces, as well as heavier mortars, that might fit the bill and be generally useful in Up Front. You can extrapolate the formulas for infantry PCs (look at the mortars) to come up with a pretty fair value for these. For tanks, the only thing that makes sense in the game is light armor that could be used in F, so I'd focus on the various armored trucks and Soviet and German-built armored cars and light tanks they had available. Some of these are the same vehicle as is in another nationality's inventory. If you're designing your NRA special rules suite to put them on par roughly with the Soviets in terms of hand rules and special capabilities, just copy & paste the stats and then mark the point value of a British or German vehicle down by 20%. If you want to ding their crew morale down to 4 from 5 add about another 15-20% to the discount. The point values for light tanks that are armed mostly with an MG or small gun and have light armor are the closest to being rational, and if you use them just to re-build scenarios E and F, it'll work out OK. Then if you want to include (say) lend-lease Shermans for X and Y Force, you'll just need to put them into a variation of scenario G or H and then playtest it until the balance is right. Another note: if you're designing them as a comparable to the Italians, the AH formula for infantry is broken for the Italians. The Italians are priced the same as the Soviets, but in practice are much worse. So you'd have to create another "tier" below the Soviets with a point value multiplier of .7 or something to make the DYO values fair, but this is just a design cul-de-sac. results.ground_truth_answer:
Dear Sirs,

I recently played the Italians, including personality card #28, PFC Ritondo w/ his Anti-Tank Rifle and I've got a coupla questions:

1. His "To Hit" values include bracketed values, so I assume he needs to be crewed for full use of the Anti-Tank capability, but he also has a firepower value of "1", w/ no corresponding bracketed value--can he thus be used uncrewed and still provide this firepower?

No, like all crewed weapons it may be fired when not fully crewed, but at less firepower or worse to hit # and higher malfunction rating.  It does not need to be crewed for AT capability or when used vs. Personnel.

As for use against personnel, it has 1 fp at all ranges regardless of whether if it crewed or not.  Like all ATRs.

2. Along the same lines, if he is uncrewed, but you are just using it for the firepower, and a red "5" is drawn, does he qualify for potential malfunction?  His malfunction values are "X6, ".

Yes.  If the ATR is not fully crewed (i.e.  no crewman or a pinned crewman), it has a malf rating of X5-6, which means if a Red 5 is drawn it will usually mean that weapon will be only eligible to break.  (Unless there are 2 or more X5-6 weapons, then you would draw an RPC to determine which X5-6 weapon malfunctions.) If you drew a Red 6, then the RPC includes all X6 weapons as well.

If it were crewed, then its malf is X6 and therefore it only ***potentially*** breaks on a Red 6.  (Because the RPC would include all firing weapons, crewman, malfed weapon specified in the rules.) That's  the risk of firing when it is not fully crewed.

Yes, in practice that means an X5-6 weapon (like a not fully crewed Italian ATR, Italian LMG) an actually breaks far more often than you might think.

Note all of this also true for Japanese ATR which is also a crewed weapon and breaks on the same numbers.

I am more surprised you didn't ask about the To Hit#'s this weapon, which is wrong on the AH card and chit (in different ways!)  This was corrected on the Wargamr Vault edition.

Request references and rationale, plz.

ALWAYS refer to errata on malfunction questions--the editor basically had to rewrite the entire to fix the many issues with it.

As for realism rationale, that a bug (not a feature) of all the malfunction rules.  (More weapons in firing group = less likely for each individual to break due to RPC draw.  More in the target group = more likely to break as there are more RNC draws.)  But to fix these problems would be far worse than not fixing them.

I'll start by saying "You're  welcome", to the many thanks given above.

Malfunction is one the areas of the ruled where so many ideas were included, that that when any question comes up, you can't really point to any one place in the rules.  One question leads to another...... The original errata keeper, Andy Maly, couldn't either.  Basically, my answer above is the whole errata.

I could see what AH was trying to do with malfunction rules.  They wanted different weapons (particularly uncrewed MGs) to have different rates of failure. They wanted the resolution of the attack to be have a lower effect on the remaining men in target group, but they wanted a single weapon that broke to fall silent.  They wanted FTs & captured weapons  to be very prone to failure.  They wanted the possibility of broken weapons to be permanently broken.  They wanted MG belts to temporarily jam. -  Infiltration and close combat can only performed against directly opposing or adjacent groups.
-  Generally groups are limited to A-D, except with reinforcements, team play and special scenario rules in three player scenarios.
